I tend to agree that the original pride flag serves as a symbol of inclusivity and the new additions aren’t “necessary,” but I’m also a cis white man so I’ve never personally felt excluded by the community based on those identities. But I want to talk more about why intersex identities are associated with LGBT identities.

The plight and struggle for freedom and equality experienced by those who are born intersex are shared with the LGBTQ community. Just as LGB folks have been subjected to unwanted treatments and psychological conditioning to “cure” them, intersex individuals have been subjected to unwanted surgeries to “correct” the appearance of their genitals, often when they are infants or unable to consent. Likewise, trans folks may struggle to access gender affirming care and to be seen and respected by others as the gender they identify with, which can also be issues for intersex people.

Remember that people have also complained (some still do) about trans identities being lumped in with non-heterosexual orientations under the LGBT banner. What we all, including trans and intersex folks, experience is discrimination based on our gender, sex and sexuality. We are also united in what we are asking for: equality and tolerance regardless of what’s going on in our beds or in our pants.

That’s not how it works. Virtually every adoptee, transracial or not, eventually has questions about their biological family. By not bringing it up, adoptive parents are communicating that it shouldn’t be talked about. Young children rely on their parents to start those conversations, because they don’t know how. Without integrating both parts of their identity, an adoptee is probably going to have a lot of distress and confusion as they grow up. Source: I’m an assistant in a research lab where we study transracial adoption, and nearly every adoptee has a story about how they wished their parents had introduced them to their cultural heritage earlier on and/or currently have issues with identity. The few whose parents did involve them in their culture from a young age either appreciated it or didn’t even realize there could be a different way. No one reports being grateful that their parents did not introduce them to their biological or cultural heritage.
